abstract: Root anatomical traits influence resource acquisition, metabolic costs, hydraulic conductance, and stress adaptation in cereal crops. Although classified as a single root class, nodal roots may differ anatomically according to their position along the culm. As shown in maize, this variation is particularly notable in root cross-sectional area (RxA). However, it remains unclear whether these differences reflect developmental differentiation or simply variation associated with RxA. We quantified root anatomical traits across four main-culm nodes (basal to apical) in 190 hexaploid wheat genotypes grown under field and greenhouse conditions. To distinguish RxA-dependent from RxA-independent anatomical variation, we applied allometric size correction, adjusting traits to a reference RxA, and conducted parallel genome-wide association studies (GWAS) using raw and size-corrected traits. Raw measurements revealed increases in RxA and cortical area from basal to apical nodes, accompanied by decreases in metaxylem area. After correction to a common reference RxA within each environment, anatomical differences among nodal positions persisted, with roots emerging from more apical nodes exhibiting smaller stele and metaxylem areas. Differences in cortical area were primarily associated with greater cortical cell file layer number rather than increased mean cortical cell diameter. GWAS identified largely distinct genetic associations for raw and RxA-corrected anatomical traits, varying across nodal positions and environments. Together, these findings demonstrate that anatomical variation across the wheat nodal root system cannot be explained by RxA alone. Our results highlight nodal position and allometric scaling as important considerations for anatomical phenotyping and distinguishing genetic associations with overall root cross-sectional area from those with tissue organisation.
